description: Earth in Counterpoint transforms NASA Earth observation data and scientific visualizations into multisensory experiences. Users explore environmental phenomena, compare changes over time, and hear selected data through deterministic sound synthesis, mapping variations to pitch, timbre, and stereo position. Synchronized text and real-time audio visualization connect each sound to its underlying data. Our mission: make environmental change not only visible, but audible.
summary: Earth in Counterpoint is an interactive web platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge “The Earth Information Jukebox.” It connects NASA Earth science visualizations with deterministic, data-driven sound, offering a complementary way to explore environmental change. Users can browse NASA visualization resources, compare supported moments or periods, and explore the global temperature record using NASA GISTEMP v4 data. The sonification engine maps temperature anomalies to sound parameters such as pitch, harmonic brightness, filtering, and stereo position. Synchronized text and real-time audio visualization help explain what users are hearing. By combining visual, auditory, and textual interpretation, the project aims to make Earth science more engaging and approachable.
details:
Earth in Counterpoint is an interactive web application that explores how environmental change can be understood through both sight and sound. Developed for “The Earth Information Jukebox,” it connects NASA Earth Information Center resources and NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) visualizations with a deterministic sonification engine.

Users can browse a catalog of NASA visualizations, select supported datasets or time periods, compare visual materials, and explore the historical global temperature record. For the temperature experience, the application uses NASA GISTEMP v4 annual anomalies (1880-2025). The sonification engine maps the numerical anomaly series to sound parameters: fundamental pitch, harmonic brightness, filter behavior, and stereo panning. The same data and settings produce the same sound sequence. Users control playback and can follow a real-time spectrum or waveform display alongside synchronized explanatory text.

The project distinguishes physical measurements from image-derived comparisons. Temperature anomalies are expressed in degrees Celsius; differences calculated from visualization pixels are treated as visual metrics, not as direct physical measurements. The catalog also identifies when a visualization does not provide the temporal or numerical data needed for a particular sonification method.

The application was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, and the Web Audio API. It also includes Portuguese and English interfaces and synchronized text designed to support users who benefit from auditory or textual interpretation.

Generative AI tools assisted with coding, debugging, documentation, and text refinement. An AI image-generation tool was also used to create the project logo. The scientific data, transformations, and sound mappings are based on identified sources and deterministic application logic.

Our goal is to make NASA Earth science resources more engaging and approachable by adding an explanatory auditory layer to scientific visualizations - not to replace the original data or visual evidence.
